title: Takeoff and Landing Performance — Charts, Factors, and Obstacle Clearance

questions.text: A pilot's POH shows: Takeoff Ground Roll = 820 feet, Takeoff Distance Over 50-Foot Obstacle = 1,520 feet. Available runway is 1,100 feet with a 45-foot tree line at the runway end. Can the pilot safely depart?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — the ground roll of 820 feet is well within the 1,100-foot available runway; the aircraft will be airborne with 280 feet to spare before the tree line; POH ground roll figures include obstacle clearance margins for obstacles up to 50 feet

options.label: B
options.text: Yes — only the accelerate-stop distance determines whether a departure is safe; if the 1,100-foot runway accommodates the accelerate-stop distance from the POH, all performance requirements are met regardless of obstacle clearance charts

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — the 45-foot tree line is below the 50-foot obstacle clearance threshold used in POH charts; since trees are 45 feet, the pilot applies the ground roll chart rather than the 50-foot obstacle chart; at 820 feet ground roll vs. 1,100 feet available, the departure is safe

options.label: D
options.text: No — for obstacle clearance, the relevant number is the TAKEOFF DISTANCE OVER 50-FOOT OBSTACLE (1,520 feet), not the ground roll; the aircraft will lift off at around 820 feet but will require 1,520 feet from brake release to clear a 50-foot obstacle at the runway end; with only 1,100 feet of runway, the aircraft will not achieve 50-foot obstacle clearance and may strike the 45-foot trees

questions.explanation: This is the single most critical performance chart distinction in private pilot training. The ground roll (820 feet) tells you only when the wheels leave the pavement — the aircraft is airborne near the runway end. But the aircraft is still accelerating and climbing close to the ground for many hundreds of feet after liftoff. The 50-foot obstacle distance (1,520 feet) tells you how far from brake release the aircraft will be at 50 feet AGL. With 1,100 feet of runway and the tree line at the runway end, the aircraft will be at approximately 25-35 feet AGL when it reaches the trees — based on the climb gradient indicated by the ground roll to 50-foot obstacle distance ratio. The 45-foot trees will be a hazard — close to or above aircraft altitude at that point. Option A confuses ground roll with obstacle clearance — the most dangerous chart-reading error in GA. Option C invents a 'below 50 feet so use different chart' provision — there is no such provision; a 45-foot obstacle is adequately represented by the 50-foot obstacle chart (conservative). Option D misapplies accelerate-stop distance as the departure safety check.

questions.text: A pilot's POH shows a takeoff distance over a 50-foot obstacle of 1,400 feet at standard conditions (sea level, 59°F, no wind, paved level runway). Actual conditions: 10-knot tailwind, wet grass surface, upslope runway of 1.5%. Using conservative rules of thumb, approximately how does this affect the takeoff distance?

options.label: A
options.text: The tailwind decreases distance, the wet grass increases it, and the upslope decreases it; the net effect is approximately ±5% — the 1,400-foot chart value remains a reliable baseline within a 10% margin of safety for planning purposes

options.label: B
options.text: Each adverse factor adds a fixed 200 feet to the baseline; three adverse factors add 600 feet total; adjusted distance = 1,400 + 600 = 2,000 feet; the linear addition method is the FAA-standard approach to performance correction under Advisory Circular 23-8B

options.label: C
options.text: Each factor INCREASES takeoff distance from the chart baseline: tailwind (+25-30%), wet grass (+20%), upslope (+10%); compounding roughly: 1,400 × 1.30 × 1.20 × 1.10 ≈ 2,418 feet; actual conditions could require nearly 2,500 feet — 78% more than the chart value for POH standard conditions

options.label: D
options.text: Only density altitude matters for performance correction; wind, slope, and surface are secondary factors that affect the pilot's technique but do not change the POH chart-based distance calculation; the 1,400-foot figure stands at any temperature and pressure altitude

questions.explanation: All three conditions in this scenario INCREASE takeoff distance from the chart baseline: (1) Tailwind: a 10-knot tailwind on an aircraft that rotates at approximately 55-60 knots is approximately 17-18% of rotation speed. Rule: a 10-knot tailwind typically increases takeoff distance by 20-30%. Estimate +25%: 1,400 × 1.25 = 1,750 feet. (2) Wet grass: increases rolling resistance by 15-25% over paved surface. Estimate +20%: 1,750 × 1.20 = 2,100 feet. (3) Upslope 1.5%: upslope increases takeoff distance approximately 7% per 1% slope. 1.5% × 7% = 10.5%. Estimate +10%: 2,100 × 1.10 = 2,310 feet. Compounded total: approximately 2,300-2,500 feet — 65-78% more than the chart value. Option A falsely claims tailwind helps (tailwind ALWAYS hurts takeoff performance) and grossly underestimates the compounded penalty. Option C invents a 'linear addition of 200 feet per factor' method that has no regulatory basis. Option D falsely reduces performance variables to density altitude only — wind, slope, and surface are explicitly required corrections per POH and 14 CFR 91.103.

questions.text: A pilot crosses the runway threshold 12 knots above the published Vref of 65 knots (crossing at 77 knots). The POH landing roll at Vref = 650 feet. The runway remaining is 900 feet. Which most accurately describes what will happen?

options.label: A
options.text: The pilot should apply maximum braking immediately on crossing the threshold  ('fly it on') to maximize braking distance and compensate for the speed excess; maximum braking from the threshold position with 900 feet available will stop the aircraft within the charted 650-foot distance regardless of approach speed

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot should be able to stop — the extra speed will bleed off in the first 100-150 feet of float; by the time the aircraft touches down at the normal touchdown zone, speed will be back to Vref; the 900-foot remaining runway is adequate for a normal 650-foot landing roll

options.label: C
options.text: The landing roll will increase by approximately 38-40% due to the excess kinetic energy — since landing distance scales as speed SQUARED, the speed ratio (77/65)² = (1.185)² ≈ 1.40; estimated landing roll = 650 × 1.40 = 910 feet; this already exceeds the 900 feet remaining before touchdown; adding float distance from excess approach speed means the aircraft will very likely overrun the runway

options.label: D
options.text: The 12-knot excess increases landing distance by a fixed 120 feet (10 feet per knot of excess speed is the FAA standard approximation from AC 91-79A); 650 + 120 = 770 feet required; with 900 feet remaining the pilot has adequate margin to land and stop

questions.explanation: Landing distance scales with the SQUARE of approach speed — this is non-negotiable physics. The calculation: speed ratio = 77/65 = 1.185. Square it: 1.185² = 1.404. Landing roll = 650 × 1.40 ≈ 910 feet. This is already the ROLL distance — before accounting for any float during which the aircraft is still above the runway and consuming pavement. Float at 77 knots (12 knots excess) on a 65-knot aircraft may add 100-200 feet of runway consumed before touchdown. Total stopping required: approximately 1,100-1,200 feet from just past the threshold. Available: 900 feet. Overrun is the expected outcome. The correct action upon recognizing 12-knot excess airspeed: GO-AROUND before committing to landing. Re-enter the pattern, fly a stabilized approach, cross Vref at Vref. Option A dramatically underestimates the float distance — at 12 knots excess, float is significant, not negligible. Option C invents 'maximum braking from the threshold' as a recovery technique — aircraft cannot brake while flying above the runway. Option D invents a '10 feet per knot' linear formula that ignores the squared relationship of energy to velocity.

questions.text: A pilot is departing from a short runway (1,800 feet) with trees at the departure end. Which short-field departure technique is most appropriate, according to POH Section 4 guidance?

options.label: A
options.text: Flap setting per POH short-field procedure (often 10°), hold brakes at full power, release and accelerate to Vx (best angle of climb), rotate, climb at Vx to clear the obstacle, then transition to Vy; Vx provides the maximum altitude gain per distance traveled — the correct speed for obstacle clearance not Vy

options.label: B
options.text: Maximum flaps (30°), rotate at the lowest possible speed to leave the ground early, then accelerate to Vy in ground effect with the aircraft just above the trees; using maximum flap deflection reduces liftoff speed most aggressively and provides the best obstacle clearance

options.label: C
options.text: No flaps, rotate at Vy to minimize drag during the climb phase; the absence of flap drag keeps acceleration maximally efficient; Vy provides the best altitude gain per unit time which is the critical relationship for clearing fixed-distance obstacles

options.label: D
options.text: Maximum flaps (30°), rotate at Vso × 1.3 (standard Vref), climb at Vy to the obstacle; Vy gives the best rate of climb in feet per minute; since obstacle distance from the runway end is fixed, feet-per-minute climb rate is more important than feet-per-nautical-mile for obstacle clearance

questions.explanation: Short field departure procedure (standard for most light aircraft): (1) Flap setting: per POH — often 10° for Cessna 172, not maximum. Maximum flaps (30°) create excessive drag that hurts climb performance after liftoff. (2) Position: use every inch of runway — start at the very beginning. (3) Full power: held at brakes before release. (4) Rotate at Vx: the Best Angle of Climb speed gives the maximum altitude gain per unit of DISTANCE TRAVELED — critical for clearing an obstacle at a fixed distance from the runway end. (5) Climb at Vx: maintain until the obstacle is cleared. (6) Transition to Vy: after clearing obstacle, transition to best RATE (Vy) for efficient enroute climb. Option A correctly notes maximum flaps but uses incorrect logic — maximum flap deflection (30° on a Cessna 172) increases lift at low speeds but generates so much drag that climb performance after liftoff is severely reduced. Option C (no flaps, Vy) misapplies Vy for obstacle clearance. Vy maximizes altitude RATE (feet per minute) — useful for climbing away from terrain where distance to obstacle is not fixed. For a fixed-distance obstacle, Vx is the correct speed. Option D uses maximum flaps AND Vy — double error: too much flap drag, wrong speed for obstacle clearance.

questions.text: At 600 feet AGL on final approach, the airspeed is 15 knots above Vref and the aircraft is high on the glidepath. The runway is 2,500 feet long. What is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduce power to idle and slip the aircraft aggressively to dissipate altitude and airspeed simultaneously; a forward slip at 600 feet AGL will restabilize the approach by 300 feet AGL, which provides adequate runway to land and stop within the 2,500-foot available runway

options.label: B
options.text: Execute an immediate go-around — by 500 feet AGL, the approach must be stabilized; being 15 knots above Vref and high on the glidepath at 600 feet does not meet stabilized approach criteria; the correct and only safe response is a go-around and re-entry into the pattern for a new approach

options.label: C
options.text: Continue the approach — at 600 feet AGL there is sufficient altitude to bleed off excess airspeed and correct the high glidepath; an experienced pilot can restabilize an unstabilized approach in the final 600 feet using power reduction and attention to speed control

options.label: D
options.text: Apply maximum braking pressure immediately — once over the threshold, maximum braking from the first available point compensates for approach speed excesses of up to 20 knots above Vref without overrunning a 2,500-foot runway

questions.explanation: The stabilized approach standard (per AC 91-79B and universal checkride standards): by 500 feet AGL on a VFR approach, the aircraft must be stabilized: within 10 knots of Vref, on the correct glidepath, in landing configuration with power stabilized. At 600 feet AGL — one foot above the gate — the aircraft is 15 knots above Vref AND high. This approach fails the stabilized criteria on two parameters. The only correct action is an immediate go-around. The go-around decision requires NO further analysis: unstabilized at 500-foot gate = mandatory go-around. This is reinforced in every airlines, military, and civilian professional operating procedure worldwide because the accident data from continued unstabilized approaches is conclusive. NTSB runway overrun and hard landing accident analyses consistently identify continued unstabilized approaches as a primary causal factor. Option A 'continues the approach' — the most common fatal decision in the overrun accident sequence. Option C invents a 'maximum braking compensates for approach speed' technique — aircraft cannot brake while airborne and still must cover float distance before touchdown. Option D describes aggressive slipping as a recovery technique — while a slip can dissipate altitude, doing so aggressively at 600 feet with 15 knots excess adds additional instability.

questions.text: Under 14 CFR 91.103, which of the following is a REQUIRED preflight action for a cross-country VFR flight to an unfamiliar airport?

options.label: A
options.text: Completion of the FAA-published pre-takeoff checklist (FAA Form 8240-6) for each runway at the destination airport; this form is available on the FAA website and must be signed by the PIC and the destination airport's TSA representative before Part 91 cross-country operations are authorized

options.label: B
options.text: Review of available runway length information and aircraft performance data from the POH or AFM for the airports of intended use; 14 CFR 91.103(b) specifically requires familiarity with runway lengths and aircraft performance data before flight; the specific calculation methodology is not prescribed but the data review is legally required

options.label: C
options.text: Filing a VFR flight plan that includes the performance calculation as an attachment — all cross-country VFR flights over 50 NM require a filed flight plan under 14 CFR 91.153, and the flight plan must include performance attachment data from Section 5 of the POH

options.label: D
options.text: At least a mental estimate of takeoff and landing distances — a formal calculation is only legally required for flights under FAR Parts 121 and 135; Part 91 private operations require only 'situational awareness' of performance limitations, not documented calculations

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.103 establishes the preflight action requirement for PICs. Specifically, 91.103(b) states: 'Each pilot in command shall, before beginning a flight, become familiar with all available information concerning that flight. This information must include... for a flight not under instrument flight rules, the runway lengths at airports of intended use, and the aircraft performance information necessary to determine whether a takeoff and landing can be made.' This regulation unambiguously requires pilots to review runway lengths and aircraft performance data — not merely have 'situational awareness.' The regulation does not mandate a specific calculation format (paper, EFB, mental), but the review of performance data is legally required. Option A falsely relegates 91.103's performance requirement to 'situational awareness' and incorrectly claims Part 91 has no documentation requirement. Option C invents a 50-NM VFR flight plan requirement (no such requirement exists — VFR flight plans are recommended, not required). Option D invents a non-existent FAA Form 8240-6 and TSA signature requirement.

questions.text: Stabilized on final at Vref, a gust causes the airspeed to spike to Vref + 18 knots at 350 feet AGL. The aircraft is on glidepath. The runway is 2,800 feet. The pilot decides 'It was just a gust — it'll bleed off in the flare and I'll land normally.' What is wrong with this decision?

options.label: A
options.text: The approach is now unstabilized below the 500-foot AGL gate — being 18 knots above Vref at 350 feet AGL violates stabilized approach criteria; the pilot should execute a go-around; gusts may persist or recur during the flare, preventing speed decay to Vref and causing float that consumes runway; the 2,800-foot runway was calculated for Vref approach speed, not Vref + 18

options.label: B
options.text: The gust is already past — since the airspeed spiked and is now returning to Vref, the approach is restabilizing; a transient gust at 350 feet AGL does not require a go-around if the aircraft is returning to Vref by 200 feet AGL; continue and monitor speed to the flare

options.label: C
options.text: The concern is only structural — 18 knots above Vref may approach the aircraft's maneuvering speed Va; the pilot should check the airspeed against Va and avoid control inputs above Va; once maneuvering speed compliance is confirmed, the approach may continue normally as the gust will dissipate

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing — gusts are accounted for in the approach speed calculation; Vref already includes a 1.3 Vso factor that provides a built-in gust allowance of 20 knots above the stall; a gust that increases speed to Vref + 18 is within the gust allowance margin and will not materially affect landing distance

questions.explanation: Being 18 knots above Vref at 350 feet AGL is an unstabilized approach below the 500-foot gate. The mandatory response is go-around. The 'it'll bleed off' rationalization is the most common mental error leading to runway overruns from gusty conditions: (1) Gusts are gusty — if a gust hit at 350 feet, another gust may hit during the flare, preventing airspeed from decaying to Vref at touchdown. (2) Energy at Vref+18: (1+18/65)² ≈ 1.30 times the kinetic energy of Vref approach. The landing roll increases 30% from energy alone. Add float distance (aircraft may not touch down at the intended touchdown zone) and the total runway consumed could easily exceed 2,800 feet. (3) Below the gate, the pilot does not have enough altitude to re-stabilize a Vref+18 approach safely — by the time the aircraft decelerates to Vref, it will be near the flare and unable to assess whether adequate runway remains. Option A invents a 'gust allowance built into Vref' — the 1.3 × Vso factor in Vref provides stall margin, not gust correction. Option C misapplies Va as the flight-limiting concern (Va protects against structural damage from abrupt control inputs, not approach speed management). Option D rationalizes continued approach from a transient gust — at 350 feet, there is no 'restabilize by 200 feet' buffer for this speed margin.
questions.sjt_rationale: Complacency and Get-There-Itis drive the 'it'll bleed off' decision. The go-around decision removes all risk. The discipline is recognizing that 500 feet AGL is the final decision point — below it, an unstabilized approach demands a go-around regardless of runway length, time remaining in the flight, or passenger inconvenience.

questions.text: A pilot is departing a mountain strip (elevation 7,200 feet, 2,400 feet long) on a warm afternoon. POH ground roll at computed DA of 10,800 feet = 2,100 feet. POH 50-foot obstacle distance = 3,500 feet. Trees start 150 feet past the runway end at approximately 40-foot height. The pilot thinks: 'I can get off in 2,100 feet and the trees are 150 feet past the end — that gives me 650 extra feet.' What is dangerously wrong with this logic?

options.label: A
options.text: Nothing is wrong — the pilot correctly identified the ground roll of 2,100 feet and the available buffer of 650 feet past the end before the trees; as long as the aircraft is airborne (wheels off the ground) before the tree line, obstacle clearance is satisfied

options.label: B
options.text: The concern is valid but the magnitude is wrong — the aircraft at ground roll 2,100 feet will be at approximately 20-25 feet AGL at the 2,250-foot point (150 feet past the runway end); since trees are 40 feet and the aircraft is at 20-25 feet, there is a 15-20 foot clearance above the trees; this is within normal departure margins for mountain strip operations

options.label: C
options.text: The calculation is wrong because the pilot used DA of 10,800 feet without applying the standard 15% safety margin required by AC 91-79B for high-elevation mountain airports; with the 15% margin: 2,100 × 1.15 = 2,415 feet ground roll, still within 2,400 feet available; the departure is borderline but legal

options.label: D
options.text: The pilot applied GROUND ROLL distance (2,100 feet) to calculate obstacle clearance, but obstacle clearance requires the 50-FOOT OBSTACLE distance (3,500 feet); the aircraft will lift off at approximately 2,100 feet but will still be climbing near ground level through the buffer zone; the 50-foot obstacle distance of 3,500 feet means the aircraft will reach 50 feet AGL approximately 3,500 feet from brake release — 2,950 feet past the runway end; the 40-foot trees at 150 feet past the end will be struck at this climb gradient

questions.explanation: This question operationalizes the ground roll vs. 50-foot obstacle distance trap in the highest-stakes possible scenario: a mountain strip with DA nearly double field elevation, minimal runway, and an imminent tree obstacle. The pilot's fatal error: using ground roll (2,100 feet) as the obstacle clearance metric. The 50-foot obstacle chart shows 3,500 feet required to reach 50 feet AGL. This means: at the 2,100-foot mark, wheels leave the ground (barely, with minimal climb gradient at 10,800-foot DA). At the 2,250-foot mark (150 feet past the end), the aircraft is climbing at approximately 2-5 feet per 100 feet of horizontal distance at this DA — meaning it is perhaps 3-10 feet AGL. The 40-foot trees will be hit. The only safe option: depart in cooler morning temperatures when DA drops substantially, reduce aircraft weight significantly, or choose a different departure airport. Option A validates the pilot's fatal reasoning. Option D invents an improbable 20-25 foot AGL altitude at 150 feet past the end — the climb gradient at DA 10,800 makes this geometrically impossible. Option C invents a 15% safety margin AC requirement that does not exist as a mandatory operational rule.
questions.sjt_rationale: This is the tree-strike scenario. Macho and Get-There-Itis combine with a chart-reading error to create a genuinely unsurvivable scenario. The correct ADM: when the 50-foot obstacle distance exceeds runway + buffer, the departure does not happen under current conditions.
